newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean police keep up security around cathedral.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean police keep up security around cathedral.

text.p: South Korean police kept a tight security net around a Seoul cathedral on Sunday where seven union leaders protesting against a controversial new labour law are sheltering from arrest, witnesses said.

They said authorities had not loosened their grip around Myongdong Cathedral, even though leaders of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions have backed away from calls for indefinite strikes.
Riot police guarded alleyways leading to the church, preventing union activists from getting in or out.

On Saturday confederation head Kwon Young-kil said his union members would limit stoppages to every Wednesday, indicating the organisation was succumbing to government pressure to halt industrial action.

Confederation leaders said they planned several rallies later on Sunday to protest the law, which allows companies to shed workers and dismiss strikers, breaking a long-cherished tradition of life-long employment.

Most strikes have tapered off after more than three weeks of nationwide wildcat stoppages that have caused production losses of at least 2.6 trillion won ($3.1 billion) and $467 million in lost exports.

Police on Saturday arrested a shipyard unionist in the southeastern city of Ulsan, bringing to five the number of union bosses picked up since South Korean courts issued warrants for the arrest of 20 labour leaders more than a week ago.
State prosecutors have warned the strike leaders they faced arrest unless they dropped industrial action immediately.

In what has become a familiar sight in Seoul since the bill was rammed through parliament at dawn on December 26, riot police clashed briefly on Saturday with about 4,000 workers and students protesting the legislation.
President Kim Young-sam's popularity has plunged since his ruling New Korea Party railroaded the bill through parliament.
He has refused to revise or revoke the law, arguing that labour reform is crucial to trim corporate costs and improve international competitiveness.
